stem: Tuberculosis (TB), influenza and polio are examples of infectious diseases.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Explain what is meant by an infectious disease.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Name a species of organism that causes TB.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Immunity can be described as artificial or natural and passive or active.

Name the type of immunity that a mother gives to her baby through breast milk.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The influenza virus can mutate frequently to produce different strains of the virus. A new vaccine is often necessary to stimulate the production of new antibodies to these new strains.

Explain why different antibodies need to be produced to give immunity to these new strains.

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.stem: Polio is a serious viral disease affecting young children. In 1996, polio caused paralysis in more than 75000 children across Africa. A long-term vaccination programme allowed the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare that Africa was largely free of polio in 2020.
parts.text: Explain how vaccination programmes can help to control the spread of infectious diseases, such as polio.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.text:
Antibiotics, such as penicillin, do not help to prevent the spread of viral diseases, such as polio.

Explain why penicillin is not effective against viruses.
